Meeting header: 2028-04-12 15:00 PDT | Duration: ~45m | Attendees: Sophie (Redwood AE), Marcus (Redwood SE), Priya (Redwood CSM), Daniel (Rivermark ML), Aisha (Rivermark Infra), Mark (Rivermark PM)

[00:00] Sophie: hey everyone, quick check — can you hear us ok?
[00:03] Daniel: yep loud and clear, thanks Sophie.
[00:06] Marcus: great, i'll kick off with the perf numbers we ran yesterday, trying to keep this focused on TTFT and streaming since those were the big asks.
[00:15] Marcus: so baseline, host env is H100 cluster with our default kernel set, batching disabled for those single-turn inference paths. p50 around 45ms, p95 around 210ms, p99 about 480ms for the 1k token prompt set with kv-cache cold.
[00:30] Aisha: just to confirm, that was with streaming turned off?
[00:33] Marcus: correct, buffered responses. when we flip streaming on we saw TTFT drop to ~30ms p50 and p95 improve to ~150ms but p99 stayed high, often due to longer seq lengths and kernel fallbacks.
[00:48] Daniel: interesting — the p99 tail is what worries our latency SLOs. our user flows have a long-tail of generation lengths, from 20 tokens up to 1,200 tokens depending on the troubleshooting path.
[01:02] Sophie: and you shared that seq-length histogram in the drive, that helped. looks like about 12% of requests go beyond 512 tokens, which triggers different kernel paths and memory behavior.
[01:15] Mark: correct, 12% above 512, 3% above 1k. we can aggressively trim some prompts but need to be careful about loss in quality.
[01:28] Marcus: right. tuning options we discussed: enable streaming to reduce TTFT, enable kv prefix caching for repeated contexts, and force a lower-precision kernel or quantized variant for long sequences to avoid fallback to the slower path. each has tradeoffs.
[01:42] Aisha: what does forcing the quantized kernel look like operationally? will that affect accuracy?
[01:46] Marcus: operationally we can route the request to a quantized variant of the model in the same pool; accuracy delta is workload dependent, typically 1-3% on our evals for completion tasks. we recommend validating against your prompt set. it saves memory and keeps the optimized kernels engaged for long sequences.
[02:02] Daniel: could that reduce p99 from 480ms to, say, under 300ms?
[02:05] Marcus: in many of our runs yes — for sequences that previously hit a slow kernel fallback we saw p99 drop by 30-40% when using the quantized and optimized kernels. but there's nuance: if KV cache is cold you still pay for initial attention costs.
[02:20] Sophie: quick note on TTFT: streaming helps because we emit partial tokens as soon as the first autoregressive step is done; that reduces perceived latency a lot for UIs that render progressively. but for strict SLOs you care about end-to-end completion time as well.
[02:34] Mark: our product teams measure both TTFT (time to first token) and full response latency for analytics; we need TTFT under 100ms for 90% of requests, ideally.
[02:44] Marcus: doable on H100 with streaming and prefix cache warm — we saw TTFT p90 ~80-90ms in the warm runs. the main blocker is requests with huge context causing kernel fallback and memory thrash.
[02:58] Aisha: can we pre-warm the KV cache? we have several repeat flows where the prompt prefixes are identical per session.
[03:03] Marcus: yes, pre-warm cache via an explicit warm-up call or use our auto-prefix caching. for the POC we can instrument a small warm-up traffic generator to keep the common prefixes hot.
[03:12] Daniel: there's also the question of dedicated pool vs hosted. for compliance we probably need dedicated but cost is a concern — will that change latency characteristics?
[03:20] Sophie: dedicated usually improves predictability — you avoid noisy neighbors and we can tune kernel allocations. latency often improves slightly because the scheduler has more consistent batching/alloc patterns, but cost is higher.
[03:31] Mark: show us the numbers — Sophie: we'll include a pricing example and a short TCO note in the follow-up.
[03:36] Marcus: another item — sequence length engineering: you can do prefix truncation, compressing context, or hybrid approach where we run a fast classifier to detect long unnecessary context and trim it. that reduces p99 dramatically in some customers.
[03:50] Daniel: we can try a conservative truncation at 768 tokens for non-critical paths, keep critical flows at full length.
[03:57] Marcus: good plan. also kernel selection: on H100 there are optimized fused attention kernels that are great up to certain seq lengths; beyond that you hit a fallback path which is slower. our runtime can select kernels dynamically but sometimes routing to a quantized variant keeps you on the fast path.
[04:15] Aisha: can you show us the kernel traces? we'd like to see where the fallback happens.
[04:19] Marcus: yes — action item for me to run a microbench with profiling enabled and attach the kernel timeline. i'll include nvprof-style markers and our runtime logs.
[04:27] Mark: thanks. also curious about streaming and client-side UX, will partial tokens come through in the same order?
[04:32] Sophie: yes streaming is standard incremental tokens; ordering preserved. if you want safety filters we can apply them on the fly but that adds some delta to TTFT.
[04:40] Daniel: security question — if we use dedicated private deployment, how are logs/audit handled? is KMS supported?
[04:45] Sophie: yes dedicated and private both support customer-managed keys via KMS/HSM, audit logs are shipped to your SIEM, and we can configure retention and redaction policies. we'll attach the security pack in the follow-up.
[04:56] Aisha: good — please include SOC2 scope and what is covered.
[04:59] Sophie: will do.
[05:02] Marcus: back to perf: i want to propose two concrete experiments this week: 1) TTFT microbench with streaming enabled + kv-cache warm (we'll simulate your seq distribution) and 2) quantized-model run for long sequences to measure p95/p99 improvement.
[05:17] Daniel: fine. what's the expected instrumentation output? like what logs will you share?
[05:20] Marcus: i'll share p50/p90/p95/p99 latency histograms, kernel timeline, runtime logs showing kernel selection, and a summary CSV of request characteristics.
[05:29] Mark: and can you annotate which runs used prefix-warm vs cold? that's critical.
[05:33] Marcus: yes will label warm vs cold.
[05:35] Sophie: one minor ask — for the quantized route can you prepare a short eval comparing quality on your top 10 prompt templates? that will help product folks decide if the accuracy delta is acceptable.
[05:45] Daniel: we can do that on our side once you provide the quantized variant endpoint.
[05:48] Marcus: we'll spin up a quantized variant in the POC pool, run the long-seq traces, and output a quality delta report.
[05:55] Mark: timeline?
[05:57] Sophie: we'll aim to get the logs and pricing over the next 48 hours and the microbench by Friday.
[06:03] Priya: i'll schedule the kernel deep-dive for 2028-04-19 10am PT — invite will go out after this call.
[06:11] Aisha: sounds good. one more question on fallback policies — can Redwood automatically route to a faster smaller model when latency is high?
[06:18] Marcus: yes policy-based routing is supported; you can set thresholds on response time or queue depth to fallback to a smaller model or cached answer. we recommend canary testing that.
[06:30] Mark: if that exists, we should test it as a mitigation to high p99 spikes during traffic surges.
[06:35] Sophie: noted. ok let's do a quick recap of decisions and next steps.
[06:40] Sophie: decisions: enable streaming for TTFT improvements, run quantized model for long seq lines, implement prefix warm for common flows, evaluate truncation at 768 for non-critical paths, dedicated pool as preferred for compliance.
[06:55] Sophie: next steps: Marcus will run TTFT microbench (due 2028-04-15); Sophie will send pricing + security docs (due 2028-04-14); Aisha will upload traces (due 2028-04-14); Priya will schedule kernel deep-dive (invite by 2028-04-16).
[07:10] Daniel: thanks everyone, this was helpful. we'll review the quantized quality report when available.
[07:15] Sophie: thanks all, we'll follow up in email with the artifacts. bye.
